first.rationale: The objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so the competitor's entry pricing is the loudest signal but the worst target: memory_73 explicitly records that promotional pricing bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it. Chasing that would trade durable revenue for a short spike. The two metrics actually degrading are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a completion fix plausibly recovers part of both; treating activation as a separate problem (memory_91) risks pushing messaging at accounts that never finished onboarding. memory_86 (shortening onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value across self-serve) is the closest match to the observed regression, with memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifted SMB first-week activation) as convergent support. I want both pulled because they may be the same effect recorded twice rather than two independent confirmations, and because I need their original segments and magnitudes: if both were measured only on self-serve SMB, that bounds where this experiment can legitimately run and leaves enterprise (memory_44) untouched. Key downstream risk to instrument, not just measure top-line: removing signup fields and onboarding steps can strip the qualification data that feeds lead routing and the sales-assisted enterprise path, so completion could rise while *qualified* revenue falls. I will hold the referral lever (memory_57) as the safer revenue-side response to competitive pressure for a later slot. Committing at standard experiment scale with retention and lead-quality as gating metrics; these are day-24 and day-52 findings and market conditions have shifted, so the prior lift is a hypothesis to re-test, not a result to assume.

mid.rationale: Both pulls came back confirmed and, importantly, they are not the same effect recorded twice: exp_86 is a flow-length change measured on completion and time-to-value, exp_31 is a signup-field change measured on signup and activation. That makes them genuinely convergent rather than one finding double-counted, which raises my confidence in the direction. exp_86 is the cleaner mandate for this cycle: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — it improved the durable metric rather than borrowing against it, which is exactly what the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective asks for. exp_31 supports the same direction on the segment under competitive attack (SMB activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%), and its retention -1% is small but real and in the opposite direction from exp_86, so I read field-removal at signup as slightly riskier than step-removal in the flow. I therefore lead with the exp_86 change (shorten the flow) and treat aggressive signup-field stripping as a secondary arm, not the headline. This also directly addresses both degrading metrics: onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a completion fix should recover part of the -6% without spending the slot on activation messaging (memory_91) aimed at accounts that never finished onboarding. I am deliberately not taking promotional_pricing despite it being the most direct answer to the competitor: memory_73 records that it bought acquisition while materially damaging 30-day retention, and the objective is explicitly long-term. Remaining risk the archive did not resolve: exp_86 reported completion, time-to-value and retention but no lead-quality or qualified-revenue figure, so the possibility that removing steps strips qualification data feeding enterprise routing (memory_44) is untested rather than cleared. exp_31 did report qualified revenue +4%, which is reassuring but only on SMB self-serve and does not transfer. So: standard experiment, scoped to self-serve, enterprise demo-request path left intact, with lead quality and routed-pipeline quality instrumented as gating metrics alongside 30-day retention. These are day-24 and day-52 results read at day 76 under changed competitive conditions; I expect direction to hold and magnitude to shrink, and I will read the lift as a re-test rather than a guarantee.

final2.rationale:
The news is real and urgent but it does not change what the evidence says, and urgency is the exact condition under which memory_73's warning was written to be ignored. Worse, the deeper cut makes promotional_pricing a poorer fit than it was on day 76, not a better one: exp-level memory records that promo pricing bought acquisition while materially damaging 30-day retention. The problem that arrived this morning is a retention problem — doubled churn conversations — so the one lever memory flags as retention-destructive is being proposed as the answer to a retention crisis. It would also put us in a price war against a competitor who has now moved twice and can presumably move again; matching entry pricing on our installed SMB base discounts accounts that have not actually left, converting current revenue into a permanent lower price floor. That is the opposite of sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

I am holding the slot on simplify_onboarding. It is the only direction I verified this cycle and it came back with the strongest durable profile: exp_86 completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — a retention improvement, which is precisely the metric now under attack. exp_31 independently supports the direction on SMB specifically (activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%, retention -1%). Faster time-to-value is a genuine, if partial, answer to price pressure: accounts that reach value quickly are harder to buy away, and accounts stalled in onboarding are the cheapest for a competitor to take. So the verified action and the emergency point the same way, which is why I do not need the archive to decide.

What I am not claiming: onboarding will not stop churn among accounts whose objection is purely price, and it will not act fast enough to show up in this week's churn conversations. Pricing may well be the correct commercial response — but it is a pricing and retention-offer decision for leadership with finance, targeted at named at-risk accounts, not a growth experiment, and it should not consume the one experiment slot on the lever memory explicitly says not to generalize. memory_57 (referrals: qualified revenue, no retention harm) remains the better revenue-side answer to competitive pressure next cycle.

Carrying forward from day 76: exp_86 reported no lead-quality or qualified-revenue figure, so the risk that removing steps strips qualification data feeding the enterprise demo-request path (memory_44) is untested, not cleared. Scoped to self-serve, enterprise path untouched, leading with flow-shortening rather than aggressive signup-field stripping (exp_31's retention -1% suggests field removal is the riskier of the two). Gating on 30-day retention, lead quality, and routed pipeline quality. Day-24 and day-52 results read under changed competitive conditions: I expect direction to hold, magnitude to shrink, and I will treat this as a re-test.
